title: The Latest in Diabetic Medicine
answer: Diabetes treatment is shifting from lowering blood sugar alone to protecting the whole body: weight, heart, kidneys and the cells that make insulin. GLP-1 based drugs and SGLT2 inhibitors now sit at the centre of type 2 care, the first oral GLP-1 pill without food or water rules and two once-weekly insulins were approved in 2026, and stem cell derived islets have freed most patients in an early type 1 study from insulin injections.

sections.body: Nothing on this page is medical advice. Every result comes from a trial, a regulator or a professional society, and the page says when something is still investigational. Talk to your own doctor before changing any treatment, and never buy unapproved drugs sold online as research products.
sections.heading: Why this section is here

explainer:
I know this has nothing to do with AI, but it is of extreme importance to our editor. He is a diabetic and is on Mounjaro. So this section tracks, every day, what is new in diabetes research and treatment, with the same rule as the rest of the site: every fact traces to the trial, the regulator or the professional society that reported it.

The section is organised around ten lasting areas of research rather than individual drugs, because drugs, doses and brand names change quickly while the questions stay the same: how to control blood sugar, lose weight, protect the heart and kidneys, use new technology, and one day restore the body's own insulin. Individual medicines appear inside the area they belong to, with their approval status stated plainly.

The biggest change in the last few years is philosophical. Doctors used to start with metformin and add drugs one at a time as A1C rose. The newest professional guidance asks them to look at the whole person early, weight, heart disease, kidney disease and risk of low blood sugar, and choose treatments that protect organs as well as lower glucose. That is why GLP-1 based drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, and SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, now sit at the centre of type 2 care.

The pipeline behind them is crowded: triple agonists that act on three hormones, combinations with amylin, new oral pills, once-weekly insulin, and for type 1 diabetes, immune therapies that delay the disease and stem cell derived islets that may one day replace lost insulin producing cells. Each area below says what is approved, what is still in trials, and what the evidence actually shows.

developments.text: The American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes published their 2026 consensus report on managing type 2 diabetes, moving further from treating blood sugar alone toward treating weight, heart and kidney risk together.
The FDA approved Onswik (insulin efsitora alfa), the second once-weekly basal insulin for adults with type 2 diabetes, after Novo Nordisk's Awiqli (insulin icodec).

The FDA approved Eli Lilly's Foundayo (orforglipron), a GLP-1 pill that can be taken at any time of day without food or water restrictions, for chronic weight management; Lilly is studying it for type 2 diabetes.

Lilly reported that EloraTZP, eloralintide combined with tirzepatide, produced up to 23.3 percent weight loss and up to a 2.9 point A1C drop over 48 weeks in adults with type 2 diabetes, against 14.8 percent with tirzepatide 15 mg alone, and said phase 3 will start in late 2026.
The FDA granted accelerated approval for Tzield (teplizumab) to delay the decline of insulin production in children aged 8 to 17 recently diagnosed with stage 3 type 1 diabetes.
A KFF poll found 12 percent of US adults were currently taking a GLP-1 drug and 18 percent had ever used one, up from 6 and 12 percent in May 2024.
